claims.text: The target Al–Mg–Li–X alloy initially consists of a rapidly solidified, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
Room-temperature cold rolling at 20–40% thickness reduction creates a high density of dislocations or dislocation networks.
Dislocations introduced by cold rolling act as heterogeneous nucleation sites during subsequent aging.
Cold-rolling-induced dislocations lower the nucleation barrier for Mg segregation.
Cold deformation followed by aging at 450°C accelerates intermetallic-compound formation relative to aging without deformation.
Deformation-assisted aging produces fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The resulting Mg-rich precipitates are more spatially uniform and refined than those in the initial undeformed metastable state.
Precipitate refinement alters surface characteristics relevant to oxide-scale formation.
The deformation-induced microstructural evolution changes the kinetics of protective oxide-scale formation during high-temperature exposure.
The deformation-induced microstructural evolution changes the integrity and adherence of the protective oxide scale.
A fine precipitate distribution that enhances oxide-scale adhesion and continuity improves corrosion resistance.
A fine precipitate distribution that enhances oxide-scale adhesion and continuity improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Coalescence of the Mg-rich precipitates into a network disrupts the protective oxide layer.
Disruption of the oxide layer by a coalesced precipitate network deteriorates corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Cold rolling and precipitation-hardening treatments can be applied to a metastable alloy while retaining high pitting resistance and producing a multicomponent surface oxide.
Room-temperature rolling and aging at 450°C are within realistic operational limits for lightweight high-entropy alloys.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is the initial sample with neither deformation nor controlled aging, and the predicted outcome is framed relative to that initial state. The actual experimental control receives identical aging, so it is not the stated baseline. This prevents the proposed two-group comparison from separately resolving deformation effects, aging effects, and change from the initial state.
